title: A Different Plan
focus: 比较交付方案，提出可讨论的分阶段试点
story:
Daniel writes the names of all the community learning centres across the whiteboard. There are more than I can comfortably hold in my head. Under them, he draws one long line and writes 'same week?'

The question mark is small. I keep looking at it.

The notification repair has completed its additional review. We have corrected another minor logging issue and recorded the test results. The system is more reliable than it was, but my confidence has not returned at the same speed.

“We need a plan to discuss with Elena,” Daniel says. “Not another list of things we might do.”

Rui turns his pen between his fingers. “The centres have different class schedules. Doing everything in one week will make support busy.”

“It also limits how long we maintain two ways of working,” Daniel says.

I have written a suggestion in my notebook. The words look reasonable there, where nobody can disagree with them.

“What if we started with one centre?” I ask.

Daniel looks at me. “As a pilot?”

“Yes. A limited pilot. We could watch the actual work more closely and find problems before involving all the centres.”

“And how long would that take?”

“I don't know yet. We'd need to agree what we're trying to learn and how the centre would take part.”

Daniel leans back. “I'm willing to consider it, but we can't keep calling uncertainty a plan.”

I close the notebook halfway, then open it again.

“Could I compare the options for the client discussion? Including the extra work a pilot creates?”

He considers this. “By tomorrow afternoon. Keep it short.”

Rui and I take the small meeting room after lunch. Instead of starting with a presentation, we draw the current staff journey: find the class, change the record, tell learners, check whether anyone needs more help.

“Whose job is this last part?” I ask.

“Probably centre staff.”

Rui turns my notebook round. “Let's try it. I'll be a tutor. You're on the desk. My room's full of chairs with wet paint. I need the other room.”

“That's a very strange centre.”

“Excellent chairs. Terrible planning.”

I change the room on a sheet of paper. He holds out his hand for the other sheet. I haven't touched it.

“Somebody at your old desk still thinks I'm teaching among the chairs,” he says.

We try again. This time I remember both sheets, but when he asks which one I changed first I can't tell. It takes thirty seconds for two people who made up the problem to lose track of it.

I cross out easy to manage. Under the three choices I write what each would ask of a person alone at a desk. If we introduce the system everywhere, everybody learns at once. If we wait, everybody keeps doing today's work. If we choose one centre, somebody there becomes the link between two ways of working. I can give Daniel the choices. I don't know the name of the person who would have to live with the third one.

In the afternoon, we test another sequence of changes and a temporary notification failure. The system records what happened, but it cannot tell us whether a learner has read an email. I add that limitation to the draft.

Rui reads over it. “Don't promise that fewer centres means fewer problems.”

“Fewer people exposed to the first problems?”

“If the scope really stays limited.”

I change the sentence.

The next day, I sit opposite Daniel with a single printed page. He reads it without speaking. I resist the urge to explain every line before he reaches it.

“You've put staff time under every option,” he says.

“It belongs under every option.”

“Fair.” He taps the pilot column. “Who chooses the centre?”

“Elena and the centre, I think. We can explain the technical requirements, but we don't know their workload.”

“What would make us stop?”

I show him a short list of proposed conditions: incorrect times, wrong recipients, or a failure staff cannot handle through an agreed fallback. None of the conditions is approved yet. We also need a reliable way to return to the existing process without losing changes.

Daniel draws a line under that point.

“That's not a small detail.”

“No. We'd have to test it and agree who makes the decision.”

He looks out through the glass wall. Someone is carrying a monitor past, walking backwards while a colleague holds the other end.

“All right,” he says. “Let's evaluate the one-centre approach with Elena. I'm not approving a launch date today.”

“I'll make that clear in the notes.”

“And send her the alternatives. She may have reasons we haven't considered.”

At the printer I find my first diagram lying face up. One centre is a little square. I try putting my thumb over it. A whole building disappears.

Rui comes up behind me. “Are you doing magic?”

“Bad magic. I can make London vanish.”

“Can you make the printer work?”

Its red light is on. We open the tray and find the back of my proposal folded like a fan. When I pull it straight the line about extra staff is almost impossible to read. I write it in again with his pen.

That is the copy I keep. Elena gets the clean version, including the option to wait. Half an hour later a reply arrives. She can give us twenty minutes between the end of one class and the start of another. There is no comment about the plan. For the first time it occurs to me that those twenty minutes already belong to somebody.

title: What the Customer Didn’t Say
focus: 发现未被说出的实际需求
story:
Elena moves closer to her camera. Behind her, a door opens and somebody passes carrying a tower of plastic cups. She waits until the door closes before speaking.

“I understand why you prefer one centre,” she says. “What I don't understand is who does the extra work.”

On my screen, our proposal looks reassuring: a small group, fewer risks, time to learn. I have spent the morning adjusting the arrows between its boxes. None of the arrows represents a person missing lunch.

Daniel leans forward. “The smaller pilot should reduce the workload.”

“For your team, perhaps.” Elena says it gently, which makes the sentence harder to dismiss. “Our reception team would be learning a new system while maintaining the old one.”

I close the diagram. Rui, beside me in the Shanghai meeting room, stops turning his pen. We had expected questions about reliability. Instead, the first question concerns the daily cost of trying something new.

“Could you take us through a normal change?” I ask. “Starting before anyone opens the software.”

Elena looks away to think. “A tutor calls in sick. A manager finds another room and another time. Reception checks who's enrolled. Some learners receive email. Others need a telephone call. Someone writes the change on the noticeboard. Then people call back with questions.”

“Does one person handle all of that?”

“Not necessarily. That's part of the problem.”

I write the steps down, leaving space between them. The empty spaces are more useful than my arrows. They give Elena somewhere to add what we have missed.

“Who decides whether a learner has been informed?” I ask.

“Sometimes nobody can tell. A message was sent, but the learner hasn't seen it. Or one receptionist made the call and another receptionist answers the callback.”

Rui turns towards the microphone. “We can show whether the email service accepted a message. We can't show that the person understood it.”

“Exactly,” Elena says. “Please don't label that as informed.”

The word is already in a draft screen. I put a square around it in my notes.

Daniel glances at the clock. We have twenty minutes left, and I recognise the movement because I make it myself when a conversation stops following my plan. He is due in another meeting. I am due to discover how little our neat proposal contains.

“There are also learners who don't use email,” Elena continues. “And people who use it but need information in a different form. A small pilot cannot mean we quietly leave those people outside it.”

My first thought is a new feature: automatic calls, perhaps, or text messages. I almost say it. Then I remember the duplicate messages in our internal test. A clever answer given too quickly can become a promise, and a promise can turn into somebody else's difficult afternoon.

“We haven't established what would help them,” I say. “Would it be possible to speak to someone at reception before we choose the group?”

Elena's shoulders relax a little. “Yes. Priya manages the centre we're considering. She'll tell you what is practical.”

“Could she join our next meeting?” Daniel asks.

“Only if we find a time when she isn't covering the desk.”

There is a short silence. Then Daniel opens his calendar rather than arguing about the slot we already booked.

We spend the remaining time discussing things that are easy to overlook: a screen shared by two staff members, an afternoon shift that starts after the morning handover, the difference between receiving a message and being able to act on it. Elena does not demand that we solve everything. She asks us to stop describing the work as though everything has already been solved.

Before we finish, I read back my notes.

“You need a way to change class times without losing track of the people who still need contact. You also need a manageable transition for staff. Have I understood that correctly?”

“Yes. And I need permission to say that a proposed pilot isn't manageable.”

I look at Daniel. He nods, though not immediately.

“Then that needs to be a decision point,” he says. “Not a comment we collect after we've announced the date.”

After the call I discover that the boxes on my diagram are locked together. When I remove the arrow marked informed, the whole bottom row slides off the page. For a minute I keep pressing undo. Then I leave the gap.

At home Maya is working on the fifth revision of a page. The first four lie on the floor in a neat row. She waves me away when I bend to pick them up.

“It's a perfectly good filing system. The oldest one is nearest the bathroom.”

I step over February, as she calls the one nearest the door. She wants ten minutes of the table and, after that, one minute of my eyes.

“I'm going to show you a page and take it away,” she says. “Tell me what you remember. Please don't tell me which colour you like.”

She holds up the page. I remember the red heading and a photograph of a woman carrying a bicycle up some steps.

“What did the woman say?”

“There were words?”

She sits down on the floor beside February. For once I have given her exactly what she asked for and it appears to have made things worse.

“Sorry,” I say.

“Don't be. I've been trying to persuade them to let her words take up half the page. Now I have a reason they might understand.”

I want to suggest moving the picture. Instead I tell her the other thing I remember: the woman's hand under the seat, taking the weight. Maya makes a pencil mark. When my minute is up she sends me off to put the rice on. Halfway to the kitchen I turn back. She is already cutting the headline in two.

title: Who Gets to Speak?
focus: 邀请参与并尊重不同表达方式
story:
Priya's first attempt to speak disappears under Daniel's introduction. Her second is covered by the soft electronic sound that announces another person joining the call. By the third, she has stopped raising her hand.

There are seven of us on screen. Four are sitting together in Shanghai, which means that our side conversations reach the microphone as a single busy sound. Priya joins from a small office at the learning centre. A coat hangs behind her. She is still wearing her name badge.

Daniel shares the revised proposal. Elena asks about the proposed group of classes. Rui answers a question about recording changes, and I add something about our tests. Our faces are small squares beside a document that seems to be speaking for us.

Priya opens her mouth. Daniel moves to the next page.

“Sorry,” I say, louder than I intend. “Before we leave that point, Priya had her hand up.”

My own face feels hot. Interrupting the person who runs the meeting still seems more dangerous than losing information. Yet we have arranged this call because Priya knows something we do not.

“Oh, yes.” Daniel stops scrolling. “Go ahead.”

There is a pause while Priya finds the microphone button.

“The afternoon staff don't all have individual email accounts,” she says. “If the invitation to the system goes to an individual account, how will they get in?”

Rui starts to answer, then stops. The proposed access arrangements assume named staff accounts. Sharing a password would hide who changed a class time, but issuing accounts also requires administrative work. Nobody has included that work in the schedule.

“That's a useful catch,” he says. “We need to arrange access before training, not during it.”

“I also have a question about training,” Priya says.

Daniel checks the agenda. I can see him deciding whether to move it to the end. I know what the end of our meetings often looks like: apologies, closing laptops, questions promised another room.

“Could we spend five minutes on the staff steps now?” I ask. “They affect whether the rest of the plan is possible.”

Daniel looks at Elena, who nods. He puts a five-minute timer beside his notes.

Priya explains that a training session at nine would exclude the afternoon team. Recording it might help, but somebody would still need to answer questions. Several staff members work short shifts. Asking them to practise outside paid hours is not a realistic plan.

I begin writing a solution in the chat, then delete it. “What would work with the shifts you already have?”

“Two short sessions,” she says. “And a written page beside the desk. Something we can follow when there's a queue.”

From our side of the table, an analyst named Noor raises a finger. She has been checking the draft instructions. When she speaks, Rui answers before she reaches the end of her sentence.

“I know,” he says. “We can simplify the screen.”

“That isn't quite what I mean.”

Rui turns back towards her. “Sorry. Finish.”

Noor points to the instructions. “They tell staff what to do when everything succeeds. They don't tell staff when to stop.”

I write that sentence down exactly.

Priya gives a brief, tired laugh. “Yes. That's the page I'd like.”

We use the rest of the five minutes to identify stopping points. If staff cannot confirm the correct class, they do not guess. If a saved change does not appear, they do not repeatedly press the same button. They use the agreed fallback and record what happened for the team to check. These are proposed instructions; we still need to test them with the centre.

When the timer rings, Daniel lets the final sentence finish. Then he says, “We need another ten minutes for decisions. Does anyone have to leave at the original time?”

Priya does. The reception desk needs her back.

We rearrange the remaining items so that she can answer the questions only she can answer. The technical discussion continues after she leaves. Before going, she offers to review the draft page on Thursday, between shifts, if we send it in advance.

Later, I ask Noor whether she wants me to invite her in earlier next time.

“Sometimes,” she says. “But don't assume I'm waiting to be rescued. I was reading the document for most of that meeting.”

“I thought you couldn't find a gap.”

“For that point, I couldn't. For the others, I didn't have anything to add.”

It is a small distinction, and an important one. I thank her for saying it. She suggests putting questions in the agenda beforehand so people can prepare a response or leave a written comment.

A message comes from Priya while Noor and I are still talking. She has found cover for the first short training session. For the second she can have Elena herself on reception, provided we finish before a tutor brings down the afternoon register.

I read the message aloud. Daniel says, “Good. So training is sorted.”

A second message arrives. Priya types fast when she can get both hands free. It says: Please ask Elena whether she's used the new desk phone.

Daniel stops with his fingers above the keys. “Is she joking?”

Nobody knows. He asks. Elena sends back a picture of the phone. A yellow slip over one button reads TRANSFER. Another, with an arrow pointing the other way, reads REALLY TRANSFER.

Noor starts laughing and has to take off her glasses. Five minutes later Elena confirms she'll come down early and practise taking a call before Priya leaves the desk. We move the invitation back to give her those five minutes.

I send Priya the new times. Her reply is one word: Lovely. A little later she adds: Especially the bit where I actually get to leave.

title: The Cost of Friday
focus: 说明选择、成本与必要条件
story:
The date is still Friday. It sits in the schedule in a green box, looking more certain than anything around it.

This is a possible pilot date, not the demonstration deadline we clarified earlier in the project. Nevertheless, I can feel the same temptation to let a tidy word stand for an untidy agreement. Friday in which place, for which work, under which conditions? We settle the time zone first. The more difficult questions remain.

Daniel places a budget sheet beside the schedule. “The centre has reserved staff time. If we move this, there is a cost.”

Rui folds his arms. “If we start before we're ready, there's a cost too.”

“I know. I need both costs on the table.”

His voice is flat rather than angry. I open the test report. We have corrected the repeated notification behaviour from the internal test, and the relevant checks now pass. That does not make every part of the pilot ready. Staff access is still being arranged, and the fallback instructions have not yet been tried by the afternoon team.

“We have two realistic choices,” I say. “A smaller, supervised pilot on Friday, if the readiness checks pass. Or a delay while we complete the wider preparation.”

“How much smaller?” Daniel asks.

“One centre, as discussed, but only two classes whose staff and learners agree to participate. We keep the existing contact process available. No automatic expansion.”

Rui looks at me. “Supervised by whom?”

“That's one of the costs.”

I turn the laptop so we can all see the empty line under support. It is uncomfortable to present a plan with blanks, but less uncomfortable than allowing somebody to mistake a blank for free labour.

We calculate the overlap between London opening hours and our working day in Shanghai. Direct support during the centre's morning would take part of our evening. Daniel can rearrange some work, but he cannot make those hours vanish. Rui already has a family commitment on Friday night. He says so without offering a detailed defence.

“I can cover the earlier period,” I say. “I can't promise the entire evening.”

Daniel writes both limits down. “We'd also need to postpone part of the reporting work. There aren't spare people waiting to do this.”

We call Elena with the two choices. She listens while Daniel explains the staffing implications. Then she asks whether two classes are enough to learn anything useful.

“Enough to observe the handover and change process,” I say. “Not enough to claim that every centre is ready.”

“And if neither class changes its time?”

“Then we learn less about real changes. We can rehearse with test data, but we should report that separately.”

She nods slowly. “Thank you for making that distinction.”

The delay has its own difficulties. Priya has already moved shifts to make training possible. A later date would mean arranging cover again. The current system causes duplicated paperwork, and another delay leaves that burden in place. Elena does not want another promise that preparation will become perfect if everyone simply waits longer.

“Could we keep adding conditions until a pilot is impossible?” she asks.

“Yes,” Rui says. “But these conditions aren't about having every feature. They're about staff being able to use the limited version safely.”

I hear the sharpness in his voice. Before Elena has to defend her question, I add, “We should distinguish essential conditions from improvements we'd like. Access and a working fallback are essential. A more convenient report can wait.”

Daniel asks me to put that distinction into the decision note. He does not choose a date on the call. Elena needs to check whether the proposed classes are suitable and whether the centre can support learners who prefer telephone contact.

Afterwards, Daniel points to the green box. “People have been planning around this for weeks.”

“I understand.”

“Do you?” He rubs his eyes. “I need something more useful than a list of reasons it might go wrong.”

The sentence lands badly. I have brought choices, costs, and conditions. For a moment I want to close the report and let him decide without me.

Instead, I say, “I think we need to discuss what you expect from my recommendation. Could we do that tomorrow, privately?”

He looks surprised, then checks his calendar. “Half past ten.”

On the train home, I reread the decision note. I remove a sentence that begins obviously. Nothing about this is obvious to everyone involved. I replace it with the evidence for the smaller option and the circumstances that would make me recommend delay.

At home, Maya asks why I am still holding my phone over my dinner.

“I have a difficult conversation tomorrow.”

“Can it happen over cold noodles?”

“No.”

“Then perhaps eat first.”

I put the phone on the counter. Maya's fifth design is face down beside the soy sauce. She has got the woman's words back onto the page, she tells me. Tomorrow somebody else will read them aloud in the client room.

“Would you like me to look again?”

“No. That's actually the trouble. Everybody gets a look. Nobody remembers whose idea it was to ask the woman in the first place.”

She twists noodles round one chopstick until they come away in a single lump. I wait. She says she would like five minutes at the review to describe the interviews herself. She can live with losing the headline. Listening to somebody else explain her research is harder.

“Five minutes in the room,” I say.

“Exactly. Can you pass the vinegar?”

My phone lights up. From across the table the screen is too small to read. I pass the vinegar. She tells me what the woman said after she put the bicycle down. It is a funny story, and halfway through it I realise Maya has had this story for weeks and I have never once asked.

title: A Difficult Conversation
focus: 区分意图与影响，协商工作边界
story:
At ten twenty-eight, I stand outside the small meeting room with a notebook that contains three opening sentences. All three sound reasonable on paper. None sounds like something I can say without reading.

Daniel arrives carrying coffee and a charging cable. “I've got half an hour,” he says.

“That should be enough.”

I sit where I can see the door, then wonder why that matters. He plugs in his laptop but leaves it closed.

“I want to explain what happened for me yesterday,” I begin. “When you said you needed more than reasons the pilot might go wrong, I felt that the choices I'd prepared weren't being considered.”

He looks down at his cup. “I was frustrated.”

“I could tell. I also became less willing to explain the remaining risks. That concerns me, because explaining them is part of my job.”

The room becomes very quiet. In the corridor, a trolley wheel makes a repeated squeak. I resist the urge to soften everything I have said with a quick apology.

Daniel takes the lid off his coffee. “I didn't mean that you should hide risks.”

“I don't think you did. I'm describing the effect, not guessing your intention.”

He nods once. “Fair.”

I had imagined a longer disagreement. The small agreement leaves me briefly without a next sentence.

“What I need,” he continues, “is a recommendation that I can take to the client and defend. The budget is limited. The centre has made arrangements. If all I say is that engineering isn't comfortable, I haven't given anyone a decision they can act on.”

“I agree. I recommend the smaller supervised pilot, provided we meet the essential checks. If we don't, I recommend a delay.”

“That still sounds conditional.”

“It is conditional. I can't honestly remove the conditions before we've checked them.”

He leans back. I can see the beginning of an answer, and then a decision to wait.

I explain the checks one by one: staff access, correct handling of a class-time change, the notification tests, a practised fallback, and a named person who can stop the pilot. We do not need every report or every improvement. We do need the people at the desk to know what happens when a step fails.

Daniel asks which checks are complete and which are not. This question is easier. I show him the evidence and the remaining owners. He points out that one owner has not agreed to the deadline. He is right. I circle the name instead of defending the document.

Then he asks, “Has the internal test problem made you too cautious?”

My first reaction is to deny it. I can still see the repeated emails in the test inbox. I remember explaining that I had assumed a new saved change should also send notices for earlier changes again. Nobody had asked me to make that assumption.

“It has made me more cautious,” I say. “I'm not sure every part of that caution is useful. But the duplicate-message checks are based on a specific failure. The staff-access concern comes from Priya. They aren't all the same kind of worry.”

“That's helpful.” He turns the notebook towards himself. “We should separate evidence from anxiety. Including mine.”

I look up.

“I worry that another delay will damage the client's trust,” he says. “I also worry about using the whole budget before we learn anything. Sometimes I push for a date because a date makes everyone organise the work.”

“And sometimes I stay quiet because I think you'll decide I'm difficult.”

“Then I assume you've agreed.”

We both stop. It is an ordinary exchange, with no dramatic revelation, but it describes months of small misunderstandings better than either of our documents.

We agree on a practical change. When a decision affects my work, I will state agreement, disagreement, or what I still need to check. Daniel will ask for that response rather than treating the absence of an objection as approval. Neither of us promises to do it perfectly.

He asks for the revised recommendation by mid-afternoon. I say I can complete it if the reporting task moves to tomorrow. He checks the schedule and accepts the trade-off.

As I gather my notebook, he says, “You were right to ask for this meeting.”

“Next time I'd prefer to ask before I'm upset.”

“That would probably help both of us.”

Back at my desk I ring the colleague whose work I offered to fit into the morning. She lets me finish. “Have you already told Daniel I can do that?”

I've spent half an hour asking him to stop taking my silence for agreement. She wasn't even in the room.

“I gave him a time. I should have rung you first.”

She can prepare an example before lunch. Checking it will take another pair of eyes after lunch. She sounds cheerful until I suggest the two things could share a line on the schedule.

“Two lines, please. Last time I gave somebody half a job they thanked me and showed the half to the client.”

When Daniel gets the new times he comes over in person. People nearby stop typing. I think he is going to ask me to find another way.

“Does she know about these times?”

“She gave them to me.”

He reads them again. “Right. I'll change what I told Elena.”

The typing starts up. I hadn't realised he had already spoken to Elena, or that he would have to make a second call because I had wanted to sound certain in the first. For a while he stays at his desk with his jacket on, waiting for London to pick up.

title: Good Enough to Launch?
focus: 依据证据作出有限上线决定
story:
On Thursday afternoon, the readiness sheet contains one empty box. Priya has tested staff access, the team has checked the limited change process, and the notification tests pass. The afternoon staff still need to practise the fallback.

Elena will not approve the pilot until that box is complete. Daniel does not ask her to overlook it. He asks when the practice can happen and whether we should tell the participating learners that Friday remains provisional.

“Yes,” she says. “They should hear the uncertainty from us.”

The practice finishes later that day. Priya sends a short account of what staff did, including a step that confused them. Noor revises the instruction page, and Priya confirms the wording with the team. We keep the original version in the record so we can see what changed.

Friday's pilot covers two classes at one centre. Participation is optional. Learners who do not want to take part continue through the existing arrangements, and telephone contact remains available to those who need or prefer it. Staff do not assume that sending an email means a learner has received the information.

Our agreement names the people responsible for support. Priya can stop using the new process at the centre. Elena owns the client decision about continuing. Daniel coordinates our response, and I cover the agreed support period from Shanghai. Rui handles a technical check earlier in the day, before his family commitment.

We also record the conditions that stop the pilot: an incorrect class time, repeated notifications, or an inability to maintain the agreed contact record. If one occurs, staff return to the existing process while we establish the facts. A restart requires an explicit agreement; it does not happen because the screen looks normal again.

By the time the centre opens in London, the sky outside our Shanghai office is turning grey. I have a bottle of water, the support number, and an uncomfortable awareness that watching a quiet screen is still work.

The first hour passes without a class-time change. Priya checks that both shifts can find the instructions. I record what we observe and avoid writing successful launch in the notes.

Then a tutor asks to move one of the participating classes to a later time. Priya confirms the arrangement and makes the change. The correct time appears. The agreed email notifications go out once. Staff begin the telephone follow-up for the learners who need it.

Twenty minutes later, Priya calls.

“We've got a handover problem,” she says. “The next receptionist can't tell which calls are complete.”

My stomach tightens. “Has anyone received a second call?”

“One learner has. She was polite, but she asked whether the class had changed again.”

The emails are not repeating. This is different from our internal test failure, but that distinction will not help the learner unless we deal with the confusion. I ask Priya to pause further calls while she checks the records with the two staff members.

They have used separate copies of the paper contact sheet. Both copies contain useful information; neither contains all of it. Our fallback instructions said to keep a contact record. They did not make clear which copy was authoritative during a shift change.

“We need one agreed record before calling anyone else,” I say. “Can the two staff members reconcile their notes together?”

“They can. I'll supervise it.”

I bring Daniel into the call. We record the pause and keep the affected class on the existing process while Priya resolves the handover. Nobody presses a button to make the problem disappear. Three people compare names and notes carefully, and the desk continues its ordinary work around them.

Priya rings us back. With the learner's permission she repeats the question that finally made sense of those two calls: “Is it still the early bus I need, or has the class moved again?” The learner has been standing at the stop with her travel card in her hand. The early bus is due in two minutes. If the class has moved again, she could wait for the next one.

“What did you say?” I ask.

“The class moved once. I read her the time. She read it back. Then she asked me to let her catch her bus.”

We have kept the affected calls paused. At reception the two people on duty now have one sheet between them. Priya asks the outgoing receptionist to show her which names still need calling. The incoming receptionist reads the same names off the same sheet. One of them spots a tick so faint it looks like a fold. They check that entry together and write the result in ink.

Elena comes to the desk. “Are you both happy to work from this copy?” We hear two separate yeses. “Then resume the calls for these two classes. Keep me here for the first one.”

On our screen nothing changes colour. In London somebody picks up a telephone.

At the end of my support period I hand over to the colleague on the rota. Rui has already left to help his family as agreed. His empty seat is a small relief: the plan has held without anyone quietly buying us another hour of his evening.

The review takes place the following week. We have evidence from one real class-time change, not a large sample. We have also learned that an apparently small instruction can affect whether people receive clear information.

Elena agrees to continue the limited pilot with the revised handover procedure. There is no decision to expand to every centre. Telephone calls, the noticeboard, and parts of the old process remain. We schedule another review and identify what evidence it needs.

When someone asks whether the pilot was a success, Daniel looks at the notes.

“It was useful,” he says. “And we have work to do.”

I save that version of the report. Outside, the rain has stopped, and the pavement is bright under the office lights.

title: The Empty Chair
focus: 清晰表达，同时为他人留出空间
story:
Several months later, a new colleague takes the seat at the end of our meeting table. His name is Sam. He places a notebook beside his laptop, aligns the edges, and says very little.

I recognise the careful arrangement of objects. Then I remind myself that I know almost nothing about him. Silence can mean uncertainty, concentration, disagreement, tiredness, or simply that someone is listening. My own history is not a reliable explanation for another person's face.

We are reviewing the next set of changes to the booking system. The limited pilot has continued, with pauses and adjustments. The handover instruction is clearer now, and staff have suggested changes that we would not have invented from our desks in Shanghai. Some learners still receive telephone calls. The noticeboard has not disappeared.

There is interest in extending the approach, but interest is not a launch decision. Elena wants evidence that another centre can support it with its actual staffing. Daniel wants an estimate that includes training and support. I want the estimate to survive contact with both of them.

Rui explains a technical dependency. I lose the middle of his explanation when two unfamiliar terms arrive in the same sentence.

“Can you say that last part another way?” I ask. “I understand what changes. I'm not clear about what has to happen first.”

He draws two boxes on the whiteboard and connects them. This time I follow. Nobody congratulates me for asking. The meeting simply becomes more useful, which is better.

When we reach the proposed staff instructions, Sam looks at his notebook. I leave a small pause.

“Sam, you reviewed these yesterday. Is there anything you'd like us to consider? You can also add a comment afterwards.”

He looks up. “I have one question. Why are there two different names for the same action?”

Noor checks the pages. One name comes from the interface and the other from the printed guide. We have been using both for so long that we no longer hear the difference.

“Good question,” she says. “There shouldn't be.”

Sam explains which wording confused him. He does not need me to explain it for him. I record the change, and we move on. At the end, when Daniel asks for final comments, Sam says he has nothing else to add. That is accepted too.

After the meeting, Daniel asks whether I can help Sam understand one part of the system next week. I check my tasks before answering.

“I can do forty-five minutes on Tuesday. If he needs more, we'll have to adjust the other work.”

“Tuesday works. Put it in the calendar.”

On Tuesday Sam brings both versions of the instructions. I have booked a room for forty-five minutes and prepared enough to fill twice that. He passes over the sheets before I can open my presentation.

“Could we walk in there?” he asks, pointing at the empty reception desk outside our meeting rooms. “I keep trying to imagine where the paper goes.”

I have worked beside that desk for months. From this side of it I discover that the telephone cord catches on the corner of a notebook and that an arriving visitor can read anything left facing up. We use blank sheets and fake names. Sam plays the person going off duty. He keeps his coat on.

“Why the coat?”

“Because the person leaving is already going out the door.”

We swap places. With my arm halfway into my jacket I am considerably less interested in giving him a careful account of what happened that morning. When we finish he asks whether London has the same sort of desk. I have to tell him I don't know. We send Priya one question about where the shared sheet actually lives. She'll answer when she has a free hand.

There are eleven minutes left in the booking. Sam would like them to himself to draw what he remembers. I shut my presentation and leave him the room.

At apartment 4B, I find Maya kneeling beside a cardboard tube. A large printed board leans against the sofa.

“Careful with your shoes,” she says. “There's a tiny screw somewhere, and I would like to find it before either of us does with a foot.”

I put down my bag and switch on the brighter light. We search the floor together. The screw is under the edge of the rug.

“What's all this for?” I ask.

“Our team review. I'm presenting the research section this time.” She puts the screw into a small dish. “I asked to take more responsibility for it. Now I have to finish the presentation.”

“Do you want me to look at it?”

“Tomorrow, perhaps. Tonight I want food and no opinions about slide layouts.”

“I can manage that.”

We make dinner from what each of us has agreed to share. The kitchen tap closes properly. There is no bucket beneath it. I still remember standing there on my first evening, pretending to understand a repair time that would have made me late for work.

Maya carries two plates to the table. My books occupy the second chair, stacked there after a hurried morning. I stop her before she moves them.

“I'll clear that.”

I take the books to my room and put them on the shelf. When I return, the empty chair waits beside the table. It is such an ordinary sight that I almost miss what has changed.

Maya is already eating. She tries the first line of her research section on me between mouthfuls. It starts with the woman carrying the bicycle. She taps the first line with her spoon. “That one stays.” She can't get the second sentence right. She says it three different ways before giving up and asking for water.

I tell her about Sam keeping his coat on. When I lose the English word for the narrow part of the desk, I draw the shape on the table with my finger. She moves her plate so I can finish.

“Was your new colleague comfortable?” she asks.

“I don't know yet. He asked a useful question.”

She nods. I pull out the empty chair and sit down.
